topics.title: Electrostatics
topics.subject: physics
outcomes: understand everyday effects of static electricity and explain them in terms of the build-up and transfer of electrical charge (u, s)

body.text: Rubbing certain materials together can transfer electrons from one surface to the other. The surface that gains electrons becomes negatively charged; the surface that loses electrons becomes positively charged. This build-up of charge on an insulator is called static electricity.

A charged object can attract light, uncharged objects — such as small bits of paper — because it induces an opposite charge on the near side of the object. Like charges repel each other, and opposite charges attract.

Lightning is a large-scale example of static electricity. Friction between moving bodies of air and ice particles inside a storm cloud builds up a huge charge. When the charge becomes great enough, it discharges suddenly as a lightning strike — either within the cloud, between clouds, or to the ground.
Use the PhET Balloons and Static Electricity simulation below. Rub a balloon against the sweater and see how it becomes charged, then see how it interacts with the wall and with a neutral object.
